title: Anne Juppo appointed Guest Professor at the University of Copenhagen
content:
The appointment is supported by the NordForsk-funded NordicPharmaTrain project, which promotes Nordic collaboration in pharmaceutical research, new joint projects and innovation.

The guest professorship is a 20% part-time position, and Juppo will continue in her professorship at the University of Helsinki for the remaining 80%.

In Copenhagen, Juppo will develop research collaboration between Industrial Pharmacy at the University of Helsinki and the Department of Pharmacy in Copenhagen. She will also initiate and strengthen partnerships with the pharmaceutical industry, particularly in the Medicon Valley region.

In addition, Juppo will contribute to the revision of the industrial pharmacy elements of the University of Copenhagen curriculum and supervise doctoral researchers and postdoctoral researchers. The aim is also to plan joint research on preparedness and resilience in the health care sector and to pursue joint funding opportunities.
snippet: The appointment is supported by the NordForsk-funded NordicPharmaTrain project, which promotes Nordic collaboration in pharmaceutical research, new joint projects and innovation.

title: Helsingin yliopistoon UNESCO-professuuri edistämään nuorten tiedeosaamista kestävään tulevaisuuteen
content:
Maija Aksela has been appointed UNESCO Chair in STEM Literacy and Future Agency for Sustainability for the period 2027–2030, a role she will combine with her research. 

Through international collaboration, the Chair aims to foster young people’s participation, hope and science skills for a sustainable future, and encourage them to study STEM subjects: science, technology, engineering and mathematics. 

“Young people want to understand the major sustainability challenges of our time, but above all they want to understand the opportunities that science and innovation offer, and to help solve those challenges in the future,” says Professor Aksela. 

The Chair’s main research and development project will be the LUMA Stars programme, a multidisciplinary international collaboration involving seven other countries besides Finland. Young people taking part visit research groups, attend science camps and meet researchers at universities and companies. They also serve as science ambassadors to their peers, and plan the activities themselves. The programme also develops, together with young people, new models of continuous learning for teachers, as well as open digital learning environments.

title: Markku Kulmala named honorary doctor of the Estonian University of Life Sciences
content:
His work centres on how very small particles, called aerosols, are formed in the atmosphere. He studies how these particles affect both air quality and the climate. Kulmala has also made major contributions to understanding how the atmosphere and ecosystems interact.

He is one of the most highly cited geoscientists in the world. The university honours its honorary doctors at an academic ceremony.

title: Stressaantuneen vanhemman on vaikeampi ymmärtää lapsensa tunteita
content:
Becoming a parent is one of life’s biggest changes, and the early years are crucial for the child’s development.

“Many parents feel considerable stress during these first years. In my study, parents’ stress was linked to challenges in their child’s emotional and interaction skills at ages one and two,” says doctoral researcher Johanna Sourander of the University of Helsinki.

Sourander’s study followed 1,000 first-time fathers and mothers from pregnancy until their child turned two.

The more stressed parents were, the harder they found it to mentalise, meaning to pause and think about what they and their child were experiencing. Parental stress was linked, for example, to children’s more intense anger, difficulty calming down and tendency to withdraw from other people.

Children with less-stressed parents, by contrast, were better able to express their emotions and to make contact and interact with others.

Parental stress especially affected fathers’ ability to mentalise.

“Fathers have become far more involved in early care over recent decades, but the parenting support they receive may in some cases be scarcer than that available to mothers,” Sourander suggests.
snippet: Becoming a parent is one of life’s biggest changes, and the early years are crucial for the child’s development.

title: Luonnontieteellisen museon Elämän historia -sali sulkeutuu tammikuussa – uusi näyttely avautuu loppuvuodesta 2028
content:
The Natural History Museum’s History of Life is one of the museum’s most popular exhibitions. However, the exhibition, completed in 2008, has long been in need of an update, as it is outdated both in terms of content and exhibition technology.

– The new exhibition will present evolution and the development of biodiversity in a more spectacular and tangible way than before. This is the museum’s most significant renewal project in years, says Sanna Vuori, Head of the Public Engagement Unit at the Finnish Museum of Natural History.

The dinosaurs Giganotosaurus carolinii and Shunosaurus lii in the History of Life exhibition have become familiar to many museum visitors over the years. They will remain in the new exhibition but will be joined by never-before-seen reconstructions of prehistoric animals. Among other things, a reconstruction of the otter-like early whale Ambulocetus natans is currently being built in the museum’s conservation facilities.

title: Southnord Artfest 2026: Roots en Route
content:
Plants have always travelled – with the wind, with animals and birds, with humans. They have been carried across oceans, taken from their habitats and replanted to serve trade and empire.

Roots en Route is a multi-sensory installation by four artists who will create a multi-sensory installation in dialogue with the greenhouses – examining rootedness and displacement; asking what grows where it was planted and what survives the crossing. The African plants that fill the greenhouses carry their own histories of movement and adaptation.

Camille Norment in collaboration with Sofia Jernberg create a soundscape drawing on the insects and birds of the plants' homelands. Toubab Holmes' site-specific scent installation traces the hidden journeys of plants through the extractive system of perfumery. Charmaine Watkiss visits the botanical legacies and healing traditions of her Caribbean ancestry through large-scale drawings of Plant Warriors. Together, the three works read the botanical garden as an archive of movement, and the plants in it as things that were carried, taken and made to travel.
snippet: Plants have always travelled – with the wind, with animals and birds, with humans. They have been carried across oceans, taken from their habitats and replanted to serve trade and empire.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.

title: Roosa Laitinen tutkii, miten kasvit selviävät muuttuvassa ilmastossa
content:
I investigate how plants adapt to changes in their environment. Which genes and molecular mechanisms make this adaptation possible?

Plants have the fascinating ability, known as plasticity, to modify their traits according to changes in environment. Plants are also able to resist diseases. With my research group, I wish to understand which genetic factors underlie these processes and help plants to improve their resilience to changing conditions.

In our research, we use thale cress (Arabidopsis thaliana) and the oil plant rapeseed (Brassica napus) as model plants. We combine laboratory studies that rely on genetics and molecular biology with experiments conducted on fields and natural environments.

Knowing which genes guide plant adaptation makes it easier to assess how plants cope with the varying conditions brought about by climate change. This knowledge helps us understand and anticipate how plants will adapt to the environmental fluctuations.

The results also have practical uses, potentially helping to develop crops that are more resilient to climate change and plant diseases, thus supporting more sustainable agriculture and food production.
snippet: I investigate how plants adapt to changes in their environment. Which genes and molecular mechanisms make this adaptation possible?

title: HEPP leader Emilia Palonen named Academic of the Year 2026
content:
The award, announced on 13 November, recognises Palonen's long-standing contributions to the scientific community, particularly her commitment to open science, academic collaboration and the development of research infrastructures.

According to the Union of Research Professionals, Palonen's achievements extend well beyond her research on democracy, populism and political polarisation. Her extensive involvement in learned societies, academic organisations and science policy has contributed to strengthening the conditions for research in Finland.

Her work with the Federation of Finnish Learned Societies (TSV) and the national coordination of open science has been particularly significant in promoting accessible publishing, research transparency and academic freedom.

In the , Palonen emphasised the collective nature of scientific achievement:

"There would be no free science without the communities that sustain it."

title: Vihreän talouden aloite tuo ilmaston ja luonnon talouspäätöksiin
content:
Climate change and biodiversity loss are economic questions as well as environmental ones. Yet the knowledge needed to address them is often scattered between research, government and business. 

The Helsinki Green Economy Initiative was launched on 12 November at a COP31 side event in Antalya. It will create a platform where researchers, policymakers and businesses work together, treating climate and nature as part of economic development rather than as separate issues. 

The University of Helsinki, Aalto University and Climate Leadership Coalition are the initiative’s anchor partners. They will seek cooperation with international partners, including the London School of Economics (LSE). The initiative is under the patronage of Prime Minister Petteri Orpo. 

The initiative will build on the University of Helsinki’s strengths in ecological research, multidisciplinary expertise and long-term environmental datasets, providing a strong scientific basis for understanding the economic implications of climate change and biodiversity loss.

title: Guest lecture: Orika Komatsubara: "Material Vulnerability" in Japanese Washi-Lacquer Composite Materials
content:
Since the Industrial Revolution, rapid advances in science and technology have driven the demand for strong materials capable of boosting productivity and increasing power. Consequently, the field of materials engineering has developed, leading to the creation of numerous high-strength and highly durable materials. Plastics, a prime example of this, have enriched our lives through their excellent mouldability and durability.

The concept of “material vulnerability” possesses the power to fundamentally overturn the conventional value placed on materials, which holds that “stronger and more durable is better”.

The lecture presents an interim report on an Art-Based Research (ABR) project exploring composite materials made from Japanese paper, “washi” (和紙) and Japanese lacquer, “urushi” (漆). These two materials exemplify biodegradable polymers that are durable and decomposable, providing an intriguing vantage point from which to examine the concept of “material vulnerability”. The research project has been ongoing for two years, and involves collaboration between scientists, artists, craftspeople and humanities scholars.
